title: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it in place and return the new head. Do it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

s1_definition.profdef: In-place reversal walks the list once, and at each node redirects its `next` pointer to the previous node, carrying three references: `previous`, `current`, and a saved `next`. When the walk ends, `previous` is the new head. No new nodes are allocated, so the space is O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a chain of transaction slips, each clipped to the one that came after it. To read them newest-first, a clerk unclips each slip and re-clips it to the slip that came before, moving down the chain once. At the end, the last slip is now the front of the chain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep previous, current, and a saved next; point current back to previous each step, and previous ends as the new head.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In-place reversal walks the list once, and at each node redirects its `next` pointer to the previous node, carrying three references: `previous`, `current`, and a saved `next`. When the walk ends, `previous` is the new head. No new nodes are allocated, so the space is O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps a chain of transaction slips, each clipped to the one that came after it. To read them newest-first, a clerk unclips each slip and re-clips it to the slip that came before, moving down the chain once. At the end, the last slip is now the front of the chain.

**One line to remember:** Keep previous, current, and a saved next; point current back to previous each step, and previous ends as the new head.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm maintains three pointers. `previous` starts null, `current` starts at head. In the loop, save `next = current.next`, then reverse the link with `current.next = previous`, then advance both with `previous = current` and `current = next`. When `current` becomes null, the list is fully reversed and `previous` is the new head.

The reason the saved `next` is mandatory is that overwriting `current.next` destroys the forward link, so without saving it first you lose the rest of the list. For example reversing the slip chain `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null` yields `3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null` after three iterations.

A senior-level nuance is that the same three-pointer skeleton underlies every reversal variant: reversing a sublist, reversing in k-groups, and rotating. The only differences are where you start, where you stop, and how you re-stitch the boundaries. Recursion can also reverse a list elegantly but costs O(n) stack space, so for large production lists the iterative three-pointer version is preferred.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a customer's transaction slips as a singly linked chain in insertion order, oldest first. For a statement view Rajesh wants the slips newest-first, and because the chain can be very long the system must reverse it in place without building a second list to avoid doubling memory. This is exactly in-place linked list reversal: walk the chain once, flipping each slip's link to point at its predecessor.

The code contains a `TxnNode` class, a `TransactionList` with `reverse()`, and a demo that builds Rajesh's chain and reverses it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: chain `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null`.

Step 1: previous=null, current=node 1. Save next=node 2. Set node 1's next to null. previous=node 1, current=node 2.

Step 2: Save next=node 3. Set node 2's next to node 1. previous=node 2, current=node 3.

Step 3: Save next=null. Set node 3's next to node 2. previous=node 3, current=null. Loop ends.

Step 4: previous is node 3, the new head, giving `3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null`.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Original slip chain:  1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Reversed slip chain:  3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null
    │
    ▼
  TransactionList.reverse()  (previous, current, next)
    │ step1: 1→null         prev=1 cur=2
    │ step2: 2→1            prev=2 cur=3
    │ step3: 3→2            prev=3 cur=null
    ▼
  Output: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null  (prev is new head)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — TransactionList reversal ═══

  ┌──────────────┐ next ┌──────────────┐
  │   TxnNode    │─────→│   TxnNode    │ (links flipped in place)
  │ + slipId:int │      │ + slipId:int │
  │ + next       │      │ + next       │
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │          TransactionList          │
  │  + reverse(head:TxnNode):TxnNode  │  O(n), O(1)
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for reverse(head):
    Pre:  head may be null or any length
    Post: all next-links flipped; returns former tail as new head
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a singly linked list in place is the foundation of the whole in-place reversal pattern, and it rests on three pointers: a previous that trails behind, a current that I am working on, and a saved next so I do not lose the rest of the list when I overwrite a link. At each node I save its next, point its next back to previous, then slide previous and current forward by one. When current falls off the end as null, previous is sitting on the former tail, which is now the new head.

The saved next pointer is not optional; the instant I reassign current's next to previous I have destroyed the only forward reference to the remainder of the list, so I must capture it first. This runs in linear time and constant space, and I prefer the iterative version over recursion for production because recursion would consume linear stack space on long lists.

In my work at the National Bank of India I used this to render transaction statements newest-first. The slips were stored as a singly linked chain in oldest-first insertion order, and the chains could be very long, so building a second reversed list would have doubled memory. The three-pointer in-place reversal flipped the chain in a single pass with no extra allocation, and I always point out that this same skeleton, with different start and stop conditions, powers sublist reversal, k-group reversal, and rotation.
